title: Put it together: choosing patterns
idea: MEET review: consolidate pattern selection and recall the whole read-split-pick-check pipeline. Thinking only.

exercises.prompt: Quick recall: match each sub-problem to its pattern.
exercises.explanation: Total -> accumulate, how-many -> count, typical -> average. The core of the pattern map, recalled fast.

exercises.prompt: More recall: match each sub-problem to its pattern.
exercises.explanation: Biggest -> max, smallest -> min, keep-matches -> filter. The rest of the toolbox, firmly in hand.

exercises.prompt: Review: which pattern answers a YES/NO about presence?
exercises.explanation: Search asks 'is it in there?' — a yes/no. Output shape (yes/no) pins the pattern.

exercises.prompt: Which of these are good habits for pattern selection? (Pick all.)
options: Match the sub-problem's output shape to a pattern
Use signal words as a first guess, then confirm
Check your choice against a hand example
Pick the pattern you used last, regardless
exercises.explanation: Shape-match, signal-word guess, and hand-check are solid. Reusing last time's pattern blindly is how mismatches sneak in.

exercises.prompt: Review: order the full thinking pipeline from units 85-87.
blocks: Read the problem (goal, inputs, outputs, noise)
Split into sub-problems and order them
Pick a pattern for each sub-problem
exercises.explanation: Read, split, pick — three units, one smooth pipeline from a wordy problem to a fully-planned solution.

exercises.prompt: Review (u85): what must you know about a sub-problem before choosing its pattern?
exercises.explanation: The output drives the pattern. Knowing the sub-problem's output shape — number, list, yes/no — tells you which pattern fits.

exercises.prompt: Sub-problem: 'the average of items under 100.' Which combo?
exercises.explanation: A two-pattern combo: filter first, then average the matches. Combos are tiny decompositions of their own.

exercises.prompt: Review: a wrong pattern can give a plausible-looking but wrong KIND of answer, so checking against a hand example matters.
exercises.explanation: Yes — count vs accumulate both yield numbers. The hand example (worked in u85-style) catches a mismatch the eye might miss.

exercises.prompt: You've read, split, and pattern-mapped a problem. Several sub-problems are 'each thing vs each other thing' (like comparing every pair). What's missing from your toolbox?
options: A way to loop inside a loop — the next unit's tool
Nothing — you can already do it
exercises.explanation: Some sub-problems compare every pair or fill a grid — they need a loop inside a loop. That's exactly what Unit 88 introduces.

exercises.prompt: You've finished the three MEET units of this lap. What can you now do with a big problem?
options: Read it, split it into ordered sub-problems, and pick the right pattern for each
exercises.explanation: Read, split, pick — the full thinking pipeline is yours. Next, the TOOL unit adds nested loops for 'every pair / grid' problems.
